arXiv:1304.0634v2 [math.AG] 07 Jan 2014

Irreducibility properties of Keller maps

Michiel de Bondt Note: The first author was supported by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO). Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Radboud University Affiliation: Nijmegen, The Netherlands Affiliation: E-mail: M.deBondt@math.ru.nl    Dan Yan Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Affiliation: Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China Affiliation: E-mail: yan-dan-hi@163.com
Abstract

J ‘ e drzejewicz showed that a polynomial map over a field of characteristic zero is invertible, if and only if the corresponding endomorphism maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials. Furthermore, he showed that a polynomial map over a field of characteristic zero is a Keller map, if and only if the corresponding endomorphism maps irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials. We show that the latter endomorphism maps other square-free polynomials to square-free polynomials as well.

In connection with the above classification of invertible polynomial maps and the Jacobian Conjecture, we study irreducible properties of several types of Keller maps, to each of which the Jacobian Conjecture can be reduced. Herewith, we generalize the result of Bakalarski that the components of cubic homogeneous (unipotent) Keller maps with a symmetric Jacobian matrix are irreducible.

Furthermore, we show that the Jacobian Conjecture can even be reduced to any of these types with the extra condition that each affinely linear combination of the components of the polynomial map is irreducible. This is somewhat similar to reducing the planar Jacobian Conjecture to the so-called (planar) weak Jacobian Conjecture by Kaliman.

Keywords.

Jacobian Conjecture, Keller map, irreducible, square-free, weak Jacobian Conjecture.

MSC 2010.

14R15; 14R10; 12D05.

1 Introduction

Throughout this paper, we will write xx for the nn indeterminates x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}, where n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}. In a similar manner, we will write yy for y1,y2,…,yny_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n} and zz for z1,z2,…,znz_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{n}. KK always denotes a field of characteristic zero and K¯\bar{K} is the algebraic closure of KK. Let F=(F1,F2,…,Fm)∈K​[x]mF=(F_{1},F_{2},\ldots,F_{m})\in K[x]^{m}. Then FF corresponds to the polynomial map Kn∋v↦F⁡(v)∈KmK^{n}\ni v\mapsto F(v)\in K^{m}. Write 𝒥​F{\mathcal{J}}F for the Jacobian of FF with respect to xx, i.e.

𝒥​F:=𝒥x​F:=(∂∂x1​F1∂∂x2​F1⋯∂∂xn​F1∂∂x1​F2∂∂x2​F2⋯∂∂xn​F2⋮⋮⋮∂∂x1​Fm∂∂x2​Fm⋯∂∂xn​Fm).{\mathcal{J}}F:={\mathcal{J}}_{x}F:=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}F_{1}&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}F_{1}&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}F_{1}\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}F_{2}&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}F_{2}&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}F_{2}\\ \vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}F_{m}&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}F_{m}&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}F_{m}\end{array}\right).

Let MtM^{\mathrm{t}} denote the transpose of a matrix MM. For a single polynomial f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x], write ∇f\nabla f for the gradient of ff with respect to xx, i.e.

∇f:=∇xf:=(𝒥x​f)t=(∂∂x1​f∂∂x2​f⋮∂∂xn​f).\nabla f:=\nabla_{x}f:=({\mathcal{J}}_{x}f)^{\mathrm{t}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}f\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}f\\ \vdots\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}f\end{array}\right).

Additionally, write ℋ​f{\mathcal{H}}f for the Hessian of ff with respect to xx, i.e.

ℋ​f:=𝒥x​(∇xf)=(∂∂x1​∂∂x1​f∂∂x2​∂∂x1​f⋯∂∂xn​∂∂x1​f∂∂x1​∂∂x2​f∂∂x2​∂∂x2​f⋯∂∂xn​∂∂x2​f⋮⋮⋱⋮∂∂x1​∂∂xn​f∂∂x2​∂∂xn​f⋯∂∂xn​∂∂xn​f).{\mathcal{H}}f:={\mathcal{J}}_{x}\big(\nabla_{x}f\big)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}f&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}f&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}f\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}f&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}f&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}f\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}f&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}f&\cdots&\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}f\end{array}\right).

The well-known Jacobian Conjecture (JC for short), raised by O.H. Keller in 1939 in [Kel], states that a polynomial map F:Kn→KnF:K^{n}\rightarrow K^{n} is invertible if its Jacobian determinant det𝒥​F\det{\mathcal{J}}F is a nonzero constant. This conjecture has been attacked by many people from various research fields and remains open even for n=2n=2! (Of course, a positive answer is obvious for n=1n=1.) See [BCW] and [vdE] and the references therein for a wonderful 70-years history of this famous conjecture. The condition that det𝒥​F∈K∗\det{\mathcal{J}}F\in K^{*} is called the Keller condition and polynomial maps that satisfy this condition are called Keller maps.

Among the vast interesting and valid results, one result obtained by S.S.S. Wang in [Wan] in 1980 is that the JC holds for all polynomial maps of degree 2 in all dimensions. Another result is the reduction to degree 3, due to H. Bass, E. Connell and D. Wright in [BCW] in 1982 and A. Yagzhev in [Jag1] in 1980, which asserts that the JC is true if it holds for all polynomial maps F=x+HF=x+H, such that HH is cubic homogeneous, i.e. each component HiH_{i} of HH is either zero or a cubic form.

Upon this reduction to the cubic homogeneous case, there are two subsequent reductions, but they cannot be applied both. The first one is that additionally, HiH_{i} is a third power of a linear form for each ii, see [Dru1]. The second one, which requires that the imaginary unit i∈K{\mathrm{i}}\in K, is that 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H or equivalently 𝒥​F{\mathcal{J}}F is symmetric, see [dBvdE2]. By a special case of Poincaré’s lemma, this is the same as that F=∇fF=\nabla f and H=∇hH=\nabla h for certain polynomials f,h∈K⁡[x]f,h\in K[x]. If both HiH_{i} is a (third) power of a linear form and Hi=∂∂xi​hH_{i}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}h for each ii, then F=x+HF=x+H is tame with inverse x−Hx-H, see [dBvdE1] and [Dru2, Th. 3.4].

In [Bak1, Th. 3.7], S. Bakalarski proved the following interesting connection between invertible polynomial maps and irreducibility: a Keller map from ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} to ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} is invertible, if and only if the corresponding endomorphism maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible polynomials. K. Rusek improved this result by showing that the Keller condition is not necessary. This improved result was generalized to arbitrary fields of characteristic zero in [J ‘ e d, Th. 5.2] by P. J ‘ e drzejewicz. In [J ‘ e d, Th. 5.1], J ‘ e drzejewicz proved the following counterpart of this result: a polynomial map from KnK^{n} to KnK^{n} is a Keller map, if and only if the corresponding endomorphism maps irreducible polynomials to square-free polynomials. We shall show in the next section that for Keller maps, the corresponding endomorphism even maps all square-free polynomials to square-free polynomials.

In [Kal], S. Kaliman showed that in order to prove the JC in dimension n=2n=2 for K=ℂK={\mathbb{C}} (and hence for all KK by [vdE, Prop. 1.1.12]), one may assume that F1+cF_{1}+c is irreducible for every c∈Kc\in K. To prove the JC in dimension n≥3n\geq 3 for K=ℂK={\mathbb{C}} (and hence for all KK by [vdE, Prop. 1.1.12]), one may even assume that Fi+cF_{i}+c is irreducible for every i≤ni\leq n and c∈Kc\in K. This was proved in [KS, Th. 3]. We shall show that for the JC for all nn, one may even assume that every affinely linear combination of the components of FF is irreducible. Furthermore, we combine this reduction with several other reductions of the JC, including both reductions in the previous paragraph. See theorems 3.1 and 3.2.

In [Bak2], Bakalarski proved that each component of FF is irreducible if F=x+HF=x+H, det𝒥​F=1\det{\mathcal{J}}F=1, HH is cubic homogeneous and 𝒥​H{\mathcal{J}}H is symmetric. Notice that FiF_{i} is the image of xix_{i} under the corresponding endomorphism of FF. We will generalize this result in i) of Theorem 3.3, where we show that FiF_{i} is irreducible if 𝒥​F{\mathcal{J}}F is symmetric, det𝒥​F∈K∗\det{\mathcal{J}}F\in K^{*} and Fi=l+hF_{i}=l+h such that hh and ll are homogeneous and ∂∂xi​l∈K∗\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}l\in K^{*}. Notice that, as opposed to the result of Bakalarski, the index variable ii is free instead of bound by an universal quantifier. So the conditions on ll and hh are for FiF_{i} only, and not for the FjF_{j} with j≠ij\neq i.

Additionally, we show in Corollary 4.5 that FiF_{i} is irreducible if det𝒥​F∈K∗\det{\mathcal{J}}F\in K^{*} and the set of degrees of nonzero terms of FiF_{i} is {0,1,3}\{0,1,3\}. If we combine this result with the above-mentioned result of Theorem 3.3, we can conclude that Fi+cF_{i}+c is irreducible for all c∈Kc\in K if 𝒥​F{\mathcal{J}}F is symmetric, det𝒥​F∈K∗\det{\mathcal{J}}F\in K^{*}, and F=l+hF=l+h such that hh is cubic homogeneous, deg⁡l=1\deg l=1, and ∂∂xi​l∈K∗\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}l\in K^{*}. The latter result can also be found in i) of Theorem 3.3.

As an end of this introduction, we summarize some results in connection with coordinates. A polynomial f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] is a coordinate if there exists an invertible polynomial map F∈K​[x]nF\in K[x]^{n} such that f=F1f=F_{1}. After some partial results in [vdES] and [Jel1], Z. Jelonek proved in [Jel2] that a polynomial map over KK is invertible. if and only if the corresponding endomorphism maps coordinates to coordinates. The result of [vdES, Lm. 2.3] by H. Derksen is that a polynomial map over K¯\bar{K} is a Keller map, if and only if the corresponding endomorphism maps linear coordinates to polynomials with nowhere vanishing gradients (for instance coordinates).

Obviously, Derksen’s result is still valid if we replace ‘linear coordinates’ by ‘coordinates’. It is however not true in general that a polynomial map over KK is invertible, if and only if the corresponding endomorphism maps linear coordinates to coordinates, see [MSY] (so Derksen’s result is only valid if K=K¯K=\bar{K}). But C. Cheng and A. van den Essen proved in [CvdE, Th. 1.1], that in the case n=2n=2, it indeed suffices to show that the images of linear coordinates are coordinates. Furthermore, A. van den Essen and V. Shpilrain showed in [vdES, Th. 1.2] that Keller maps FF are invertible if F1F_{1} is a coordinate and the JC holds in dimension n−1n-1.

2 Some properties of Keller maps

We start with a generalization of [J ‘ e d, Th. 4.1] by J ‘ e drzejewicz. To be precise, [J ‘ e d, Th. 4.1] is the equivalence of 1) and 2) in the theorem below, for the case that gg is irreducible.

Let F∈K​[x]nF\in K[x]^{n} be an arbitrary polynomial map. If g∈K⁡[x]g\in K[x] is square-free, then the following conditions are equivalent:

Assume that g∈K⁡[x]g\in K[x] is square-free. The equivalence of 1) and 2) follows by applying [J ‘ e d, Th. 4.1] for all irreducible polynomials g~|g\tilde{g}\mid g. To prove 2) ⟹\Longrightarrow 3), take for ww in 3) the least common multiple of all w~\tilde{w} appearing in 2). Then w⁡(F)w(F) in 3) is a common multiple of the w~​(F)\tilde{w}(F) appearing in 2). Since g2g^{2} in 3) is the least common multiple of the g~2\tilde{g}^{2} appearing in 2), 2) ⟹\Longrightarrow 3) follows. Hence it remains to show 3) ⟹\Longrightarrow 2).

So assume 3) and let g~\tilde{g} be an arbitrary irreducible divisor of gg. We have to show that there exists an irreducible w~∈K⁡[y]\tilde{w}\in K[y] such that g~2|w~​(F)\tilde{g}^{2}\mid\tilde{w}(F). Since g2|w⁡(F)g^{2}\mid w(F), we can decompose w=w1​w2w=w_{1}w_{2}, such that w1w_{1} is irreducible and g~|w1​(F)\tilde{g}\mid w_{1}(F). If g~2|w1​(F)\tilde{g}^{2}\mid w_{1}(F), then we are done, so suppose that g~2∤w1​(F)\tilde{g}^{2}\nmid w_{1}(F). Then g~|w2​(F)\tilde{g}\mid w_{2}(F). Let F¯\bar{F} be the residue classes of FF modulo g~\tilde{g}, i.e. F¯i=Fi+(g~)\bar{F}_{i}=F_{i}+(\tilde{g}) for each ii. Define r:=trdegK⁡(F¯1,F¯2,…,F¯n)r:=\operatorname{trdeg}_{K}(\bar{F}_{1},\bar{F}_{2},\ldots,\bar{F}_{n}) and assume without loss of generality that F¯1,F¯2,…,F¯r\bar{F}_{1},\bar{F}_{2},\ldots,\bar{F}_{r} are algebraically independent over KK. If r≤n−2r\leq n-2, then we can follow the last paragraph in the proof of (i) ⟹\Longrightarrow (ii) of [J ‘ e d, Th. 4.1] verbatim to obtain that g~2|w~​(F)\tilde{g}^{2}\mid\tilde{w}(F) for some irreducible w~∈K⁡[y]\tilde{w}\in K[y]. So assume that r=n−1r=n-1. Notice that w1w_{1} and w2w_{2} are relatively prime, because ww is square-free. Hence by Krull’s Principal Ideal Theorem, the ideal (w1,w2)(w_{1},w_{2}) has height at least two. Just like [J ‘ e d, Th. 4.1], its immediate consequence [J ‘ e d, Cor. 4.2] can be generalized. We do this by extending it with one line, namely property 3).

Corollary 2.2.

Let F∈K​[x]nF\in K[x]^{n} be an arbitrary polynomial map. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. 1)

    det𝒥​F∈K∗\det{\mathcal{J}}F\in K^{*},

    for every irreducible polynomial w∈K⁡[y]w\in K[y], the polynomial w⁡(F)w(F) is square-free,

  3. 3)

    for every square-free polynomial w∈K⁡[y]w\in K[y], the polynomial w⁡(F)w(F) is square-free.

Proof.

Every assertion is equivalent to the nonexistence of an irreducible gg in the respective assertion of Theorem 2.1. ∎

We end this section with a theorem about some reducibility properties which cannot be combined with the Keller condition. We use a result of [LM] for that.

Theorem 2.3.

Let F∈K​[x]nF\in K[x]^{n} be a Keller map. Suppose that for each ii, FiF_{i} is of the form Li​HiL_{i}H_{i}, where deg⁡Li=1\deg L_{i}=1. Then the following statements are equivalent.

  1. 1)

    The linear part of Li​(0)​HiL_{i}(0)H_{i} is divisible by Li−Li​(0)L_{i}-L_{i}(0) for each ii,

  2. 2)

    L⁡(0)L(0) is contained in the column space of 𝒥​L{\mathcal{J}}L,

  3. 3)

    det𝒥​L∈K∗\det{\mathcal{J}}L\in K^{*},

  4. 4)

    deg⁡F=1\deg F=1,

  5. 5)

    FiF_{i} is irreducible for each ii.

Proof.

Notice that 3) ⟹\Longrightarrow 2) and 4) ⟺\Longleftrightarrow 5) are trivial. Hence it suffices to prove the following.

1) ⇒\Rightarrow 3)

Suppose that 1) holds. Since Fi=Li​(0)​Hi+(Li−Li​(0))​HiF_{i}=L_{i}(0)H_{i}+\big(L_{i}-L_{i}(0)\big)H_{i} for all ii, we can deduce that for each ii, the linear part of FiF_{i} is equal to (Li−Li​(0))​ci\big(L_{i}-L_{i}(0)\big)c_{i} for some ci∈Kc_{i}\in K. 2) ⇒\Rightarrow 3)

Let ∗* denote the Hadamard product and suppose that 2) holds. Say that 𝒥​L⋅a=L⁡(0){\mathcal{J}}L\cdot a=L(0), where a∈Kna\in K^{n}. Then the constant part of L⁡(x−a)L(x-a) is equal to

L⁡(−a)=𝒥​L|x=−a⋅(−a)+L⁡(0)=𝒥​L⋅(−a)+𝒥​L⋅a=0.L(-a)={\mathcal{J}}L|_{x=-a}\cdot(-a)+L(0)={\mathcal{J}}L\cdot(-a)+{\mathcal{J}}L\cdot a=0.

Hence the linear part of F⁡(x−a)=L⁡(x−a)∗H⁡(x−a)F(x-a)=L(x-a)*H(x-a) is equal to L⁡(x−a)∗H⁡(−a)L(x-a)*H(-a). Using the Keller condition for FF, det𝒥​L​∣det(𝒥​F)|x=x−a∈K∗\det{\mathcal{J}}L\mid\det({\mathcal{J}}F)|_{x=x-a}\in K^{*} follows, which is 3).

3) ⇒\Rightarrow 4)

Suppose that 3) holds. Then LL is invertible and

F⁡(L−1​(x))=L⁡(L−1​(x))∗H⁡(L−1​(x))=x∗H⁡(L−1​(x))F\big(L^{-1}(x)\big)=L\big(L^{-1}(x)\big)*H\big(L^{-1}(x)\big)=x*H\big(L^{-1}(x)\big)

is a Keller map as well. It follows from [LM, Prop. 6] that deg⁡H=deg⁡H⁡(L−1​x)=0\deg H=\deg H(L^{-1}x)=0. Hence deg⁡F=1\deg F=1.

4) ⇒\Rightarrow 1)

Suppose that deg⁡F=1\deg F=1. Then deg⁡Hi=0\deg H_{i}=0 and hence Li​(0)​Hi∈KL_{i}(0)H_{i}\in K for each ii. Thus for each ii, the linear part of Li​(0)​HiL_{i}(0)H_{i} is zero, which is divisible by Li−Li​(0)L_{i}-L_{i}(0). ∎

Proposition 3.4.

Assume that f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x] such that deg⁡f≠1\deg f\neq 1 and h:=f−xih:=f-x_{i} is a polynomial in a linear form. If h∈K⁡[xi]h\in K[x_{i}], then ff is not a component of a Keller map. If h∉K⁡[xi]h\notin K[x_{i}], then ff is a tame coordinate.

Proof.

If h∈K⁡[xi]h\in K[x_{i}], then ff cannot be a component of a Keller map because 𝒥​f{\mathcal{J}}f is not unimodular. So assume h∉K⁡[xi]h\notin K[x_{i}]. Then there exists a T∈GLn⁡(K)T\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(K) such that T1​x=xiT_{1}x=x_{i} and h∈K⁡[T2​x]h\in K[T_{2}x], say that h=p⁡(T2​x)h=p(T_{2}x). It follows that ff is the first component of the composition of the elementary invertible map (x1+p⁡(x2),x2,x3,…,xn)(x_{1}+p(x_{2}),x_{2},x_{3},\ldots,x_{n}) and TT. ∎

Proposition 3.4 is a special case of Proposition 5.6, which follows later. Just as with Proposition 3.4, the proof of Proposition 5.6 is self-contained (without references to other results).

Notice that i) of Theorem 3.3 and Proposition 3.4 are results about Keller maps of some type, rather than subsequent reductions to obtain irreducibility results. More results of this type are Theorem 5.1 and its corollary, and Theorems 6.1 and 7.3.

4 Irreducibility lemmas for polynomials with unimodular gradients

Lemma 4.1.

Let AA be a unique factorization domain and g∈A⁡[x1]g\in A[x_{1}]. Suppose that (x1−c)2​g(x_{1}-c)^{2}g has terms of degrees 00, 11 and dd only for some nonzero c∈Ac\in A. Then

(x1−c)2​g=c′​(x1d−cd)−c′​d​cd−1​(x1−c)(x_{1}-c)^{2}g=c^{\prime}(x_{1}^{d}-c^{d})-c^{\prime}dc^{d-1}(x_{1}-c) (10)

for some c′∈Ac^{\prime}\in A.

Proof.

Let c′∈Ac^{\prime}\in A be the coefficient of x1dx_{1}^{d} in (x1−c)2​g(x_{1}-c)^{2}g. Then the left hand side of (10) is of the form c′​x1d+b′​x1+a′c^{\prime}x_{1}^{d}+b^{\prime}x_{1}+a^{\prime} for some a′,b′∈Aa^{\prime},b^{\prime}\in A. Since c′c^{\prime} is already given, there is only one polynomial of the form c′​x1d+b′​x1+a′c^{\prime}x_{1}^{d}+b^{\prime}x_{1}+a^{\prime}, with a′,b′∈Aa^{\prime},b^{\prime}\in A, which is divisible by (x1−c)2(x_{1}-c)^{2}. Hence it suffices to show that the right hand side of (10) is divisible by (x1−c)2(x_{1}-c)^{2}. If we divide the right hand side of (10) by c′​(x1−c)c^{\prime}(x_{1}-c), then we get

(x1d−1+c​x1d−2+⋯+cd−1)−d​cd−1=∑i=0d−1cd−1−i​(x1i−ci),(x_{1}^{d-1}+cx_{1}^{d-2}+\cdots+c^{d-1})-dc^{d-1}=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}c^{d-1-i}(x_{1}^{i}-c^{i}),

which is again divisible by x1−cx_{1}-c. So the right hand side of (10) is divisible by x1−cx_{1}-c twice. ∎

5 Irreducibility results for arbitrary Keller maps

Theorem 5.1.

Let F∈K​[x]nF\in K[x]^{n} be a Keller map of degree dd. Take i∈{1,2,…,n,n+1}i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n,\allowbreak n+1\} and fix μ1,…,μi−1,μi+1,…,μn+1∈K¯\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{i-1},\mu_{i+1},\ldots,\mu_{n+1}\in\bar{K}. If μj≠0\mu_{j}\neq 0 for some jj with i≠j≤ni\neq j\leq n, then

f:=μ1​F1+μ2​F2+⋯+μn​Fn+μn+1f:=\mu_{1}F_{1}+\mu_{2}F_{2}+\cdots+\mu_{n}F_{n}+\mu_{n+1}

is reducible over K¯\bar{K} for at most d2−1d^{2}-1 values of μi∈K¯\mu_{i}\in\bar{K}.

Proof.

Assume without loss of generality that j=1j=1. Then (f,F2,…,Fn)(f,F_{2},\ldots,F_{n}) is a Keller map as well. By expansion of the Jacobian determinant along the first row, we see that gcd⁡{∂∂x1​f,∂∂x2​f,…,∂∂xn​f}∈K∗⊆K¯∗\gcd\big\{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{1}}f,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{2}}f,\ldots,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}f\big\}\in K^{*}\subseteq\bar{K}^{*}. Hence the case i=n+1i=n+1 follows from 2) ⟹\Longrightarrow 4) of lemma 4.6.

Lemma 7.4.

Let ff be of the form g0+g1​y1+g2​y2+⋯+gn​yn≠g0g_{0}+g_{1}y_{1}+g_{2}y_{2}+\cdots+g_{n}y_{n}\neq g_{0}, where gi∈Ag_{i}\in A for all ii for some unique factorization domain AA. Then ff is irreducible, if and only if gcd⁡{g0,g1,g2,…,gn}∈A∗\gcd\{g_{0},g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{n}\}\in A^{*}.

Proof.

If ff decomposes in two factors, then one of the factors is constant with respect to yy. The rest of the proof is an easy exercise. ∎

Lemma 7.5.

Assume that F∈K​[x]nF\in K[x]^{n} is a polynomial map over KK and f∈K⁡[x]f\in K[x]. Set G:=∇x,y(f+yt​F)G:=\nabla_{x,y}(f+y^{\mathrm{t}}F). Then det𝒥x,y​G=(−1)n​(det𝒥​F)2\det{\mathcal{J}}_{x,y}G=(-1)^{n}(\det{\mathcal{J}}F)^{2} and FF is invertible, if and only if GG is invertible. Furthermore,

whence det𝒥x,y​G=(−1)n​(det𝒥​F)2\det{\mathcal{J}}_{x,y}G=(-1)^{n}(\det{\mathcal{J}}F)^{2}. Consequently, both FF and GG are Keller maps if one of them is, which we assume from now on. Notice that G=((𝒥​F)t​y+∇f,F)G=\big(({\mathcal{J}}F)^{\mathrm{t}}y+\nabla f,F\big) by definition. Hence we have

(g1g2⋯gn)=𝒥y((μ1μ2⋯μn)((𝒥F)ty+∇f))(g_{1}~g_{2}~\cdots~g_{n})={\mathcal{J}}_{y}\Big((\mu_{1}~\mu_{2}~\cdots~\mu_{n})\big(({\mathcal{J}}F)^{\mathrm{t}}y+\nabla f\big)\Big)

is a nontrivial linear combination of the rows of (𝒥​F)t({\mathcal{J}}F)^{\mathrm{t}}, so (g1g2⋯gn)(g_{1}~g_{2}~\cdots~g_{n}) is unimodular. In particular, gcd⁡{g0,g1,g2,…,gn}∈K∗\gcd\{g_{0},g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{n}\}\in K^{*}. Hence (13) is irreducible on account of Lemma 7.4. ∎
